## Reading in Packages and Data
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(here)

# Read in geodatabase of EJScreen data at the Census Block Group level
ejscreen <- sf::st_read(here::here("data", "EJSCREEN_2023_BG_StatePct_with_AS_CNMI_GU_VI.gdb")) 

# Filter to a state I'm interested in: CA
california <- ejscreen %>%
  dplyr::filter(ST_ABBREV == "CA") 

# Filter to a county I'm interested in: LA
los_angeles <- ejscreen %>%
  dplyr::filter(CNTY_NAME %in% c("Los Angeles County"))

# Find the average values for all variables within counties
california_counties <- aggregate(california, by = list(california$CNTY_NAME), FUN = mean)
```

I decided to look at LA county because I'm from here and have lived here my whole life besides my time at UCSB. As most know, there's lots of traffic, so when I saw one of the variables was traffic proximity, I knew I wanted to do something with that. 


## Exploring the Data
```{r}
# Looking at the shape of the LA dataframe
dim(los_angeles)  # 6591 rows, 224 cols
```

## Filtering
```{r}
# Narrowing the dataframe down to 2 variables I'm interested in
la <- los_angeles |> 
    select('PTRAF', 'PM25', 'LOWINCPCT') 
```

```{r}
# Getting rid of missing values in each column
la_clean <- la |> filter(!is.na(PTRAF), !is.na(PM25), !is.na(LOWINCPCT))
```

```{r}
# Making a new variable for traffic proximity after 80th percentile
high_traffic <- la_clean |> filter(PTRAF >= quantile(PTRAF, 0.8))
```


## Graphs

### Graph 1

```{r}
# Graph 1
tm_shape(la_clean) + 
    tm_polygons(fill = 'PM25',  # bottom layer is of PM2.5
        fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(values = 'brewer.yl_or_rd'), # color scale
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = 'PM2.5 (µg/m^3)'),  # legend title
        col = 'white',  # border color change
        lwd = 0.2) +  # line width of the borders change
tm_shape(high_traffic) +  # layering high traffic on top of it
    tm_dots(fill = '#2c7fb8', size = 0.15) +  # dots with blue color and certain size
tm_add_legend(type = 'symbols',  # adding a legend for the symbols
        labels = 'Top 20% Traffic Proximity', 
        fill = '#2c7fb8') +  # same blue as before
    tm_title('PM2.5 and Traffic Proximity in LA County') +  # title for graph
tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "top"), text.size = 0.4) + # adds a scale bar
tm_compass(type = "arrow", position = c("right", "bottom"))  # adds a compass
```

This graph looks at the PM 2.5 concentration and the top 20% traffic proximity in LA County. The yellow to orange to red color scale represents the PM 2.5 levels in ascending order. The blue dots represent the top 20% traffic proximity. The dots tend to go in a line. Off an initial look, a lot of these dots that form lines appear to be freeways. I can see where the 10, 405, and 105 are located quite clearly. The cluster in the middle is Downtown LA where many of the freeways intersect. The relationship between high PM 2.5 and high traffic proximity isn't as related as I thought it would be. There's a reasonable amount of red to dark red areas without any blue dots, and there's some blue dots in yellow and light orange areas. After looking more closely at the freeways I recognize, there's a gap in one of the freeways that runs along the coast (the 405) in an orange area. Comparing this area to a map, the gap happens to be in Beverly Hills. This didn't surprise me since Beverly Hills has the reputation it has. However, this made me wonder what the communities around the blue dots look like. 


### Graph 2

```{r}
# Income map by itself
tm_shape(la_clean) + 
    tm_polygons(fill = 'LOWINCPCT',   # bottom layer is of LOWINCPCT
        fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = 'quantile', values = 'brewer.greens'),
        # quantile is to get the percentage. values is the color scale 
        fill.legend = tm_legend('% Low Income'), 
        col = 'white', 
        lwd = 0.2) + 
tm_shape(high_traffic) + 
    tm_dots(fill = '#2c7fb8', size = 0.15) +   # adding the traffic dots
tm_add_legend(type = 'symbols',  # adding a legend for the symbols
        labels = 'Top 20% Traffic Proximity',  # title
        fill = '#2c7fb8') +  # same blue as before
tm_title('Low Income') +   # title for this graph
tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom"), text.size = 0.4) +  # adds a scalebar
tm_compass(type = "arrow", position = c("right", "bottom")) # adds a compass
```

This graph compares the percentage of low income people in LA County to the top 20% traffic proximity. The light green represents a lower percentage of low income people, while the darker green represents a higher percentage of low income people. The blue dots, like above, represent the top 20% of traffic proximity. 
 


### Graphs 1 and 2 Combined

```{r}
# Graph 2
pm_map <- tm_shape(la_clean) + 
    tm_polygons(fill = 'PM25',  
        fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(values = 'brewer.yl_or_rd'), 
        fill.legend = tm_legend(title = 'PM2.5 (µg/m^3)'),  
        col = 'white',  
        lwd = 0.2) +  
tm_shape(high_traffic) +  
    tm_dots(fill = '#2c7fb8', size = 0.15) +  
tm_add_legend(type = 'symbols',  
        labels = 'Top 20% Traffic Proximity', 
        fill = '#2c7fb8') +  
tm_title('PM2.5') +  
tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom"), text.size = 0.5) +  # adds a scale bar
tm_compass(type = "arrow", position = c("right", "bottom"))  # adds a compass

income_map <- tm_shape(la_clean) + 
    tm_polygons(fill = 'LOWINCPCT', 
        fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = 'quantile', values = 'brewer.greens'), 
        fill.legend = tm_legend('% Low Income'), 
        col = 'white', 
        lwd = 0.2) + 
tm_shape(high_traffic) + 
    tm_dots(fill = '#2c7fb8', size = 0.15) + 
tm_add_legend(type = 'symbols',  
        labels = 'Top 20% Traffic Proximity',  
        fill = '#2c7fb8') +  
tm_title('Low Income')  

tmap_arrange(pm_map, income_map, ncol = 2)  
# arranges the graphs next to each other in 2 columns
```

These graphs look at the PM 2.5 concentration combined with the top 20% traffic proximity and the PM 2.5 concentration combined with the percent of low income people in LA County (from left to right). The yellow to orange to red color scale on the left graph represents the PM 2.5 levels in ascending order. The blue dots represent the top 20% traffic proximity. The dots tend to form lines that appear to be along freeways. The map on the right is the same as the green one above, 
. I put the graphs next to each other to compare PM 2.5 concentration and the percent of people in an area that are considered to be low income, while still keeping the traffic proximity dots. There doesn't appear to be a strong relationship or pattern between any of the variables, which is interesting in and of itself.
